title: Staff+ Competencies
summary: The signals that distinguish senior-IC from staff+ candidates — impact through others and systems, technical vision, and operating with organizational ambiguity, not just deeper technical skill.

slides.markdown:
A common misconception: staff engineer is just "senior engineer, but better at coding." It isn't. **What changes at staff+ is the unit of impact** — a senior IC is evaluated substantially on their own output; a staff+ engineer is evaluated on impact that runs through other people and systems, often on problems too large or ambiguous for one person to execute alone.

This topic covers what actually changes: the multiplier effect, the recognized staff archetypes, technical vision, and operating with organizational ambiguity — plus the single most common way candidates misfire on this bar: a "staff-level" story that's still scoped to one person's individual contribution.

slides.subTitle: Impact through others and systems
slides.markdown:
The core shift: a staff+ engineer's personal code output typically shrinks relative to their overall impact, because the leverage moves elsewhere — into decisions, systems, and people that scale beyond what any one person can personally build.

Concretely, a senior IC's strong quarter might be "I built and shipped the new billing service." A staff+ engineer's strong quarter might be "I set the architecture three teams are building against, unblocked a cross-team dependency that had stalled for two months, and mentored two engineers into the tech-lead role on their own projects" — none of which required the staff engineer to personally write most of the code involved.

This is why staff+ behavioral stories should sound different in kind, not just bigger — if every story is still "here's a hard thing I personally built," it may be an excellent senior-IC portfolio without yet showing the through-others pattern staff+ interviews are calibrated to look for.

"Multiplier" impact means work that scales a team's output beyond what headcount alone would produce — three common forms:

- **Mentorship** — growing another engineer's capability such that they independently produce more, or higher-quality, work going forward. Concrete evidence: an engineer you mentored who's since led their own project or been promoted.
- **Tooling** — building something once that removes recurring cost for many people. Concrete evidence: a CI check, library, or internal tool with measurable adoption and time saved.
- **Process** — a change to how a team works that improves output broadly. Concrete evidence: a review or planning process change with a measurable before/after, like cycle time or incident rate.

The common thread: in each case, the staff engineer's one-time investment keeps paying off through other people's ongoing work, rather than the impact being capped at what they alone could produce in the same hours.

Will Larson's widely-referenced framing names four common staff archetypes — useful for placing your own stories, not a rigid categorization:

| Archetype | Typical focus | Example behavior |
|---|---|---|
| **Tech lead** | driving a specific initiative or team's technical direction | leading a migration across several teams |
| **Architect** | setting technical direction for a domain | defining the data-consistency model a whole product area builds on |
| **Solver** | going deep on the org's hardest, highest-stakes problems | being the person parachuted into the most dangerous incident or riskiest launch |
| **Right-hand** | extending an executive or director's reach across many initiatives | representing leadership's priorities across teams they can't personally cover |

Most staff engineers lean toward one or two archetypes rather than doing all four equally — being able to name which one your own track record fits, and having stories that match it, reads as more self-aware than a generic "I do a bit of everything."

slides.subTitle: Setting direction across teams and quarters
slides.markdown:
Technical vision means having, and successfully advocating for, an opinion about where a technical domain should go over a longer horizon than a single project — usually multiple quarters, and usually spanning more than one team's roadmap.

Example shape: rather than reacting to each team's ad hoc request for a new data pipeline, a staff engineer notices the pattern across six months of requests, proposes a unified event-streaming architecture that the next dozen use cases can build on rather than each reinventing ingestion, and gets it adopted as the default path — not by mandate, but by making it clearly the easiest, best-supported option available.

The test an interviewer applies here: did you correctly anticipate a direction *before* it became an obvious, forced necessity, and did you get others to build toward it voluntarily. A vision that only gets articulated after the org was already forced into that direction by circumstance doesn't really demonstrate foresight.

At staff+, the ambiguity you're expected to operate in often isn't technical — it's organizational: unclear ownership between teams, a roadmap priority nobody has actually decided, two leaders with quietly conflicting goals for the same system.

Example shape: two product teams both build features that write to the same core data model, with no agreed process for coordinating schema changes, and it's caused two silent data-corruption bugs. Nobody explicitly owns "cross-team schema governance" — it's fallen in a gap between two org charts. A staff engineer operating well here doesn't wait for someone to formally assign the problem; they propose a lightweight governance process, get both teams' leads to agree to it despite neither one being told to by their own management chain, and become the de facto owner of a problem that technically belongs to no one's job description.

The skill being tested is comfort acting without a clean mandate, in a space where the org chart itself hasn't caught up to the actual problem.

"Tell me about a technical decision you drove" answered at two levels:

| | Senior-IC answer | Staff answer |
|---|---|---|
| Scope | Chose the caching strategy for one service | Set the caching strategy adopted as the default across a product area |
| Depth vs breadth | Deep, bounded ownership of one system | Breadth — the same judgment applied and defended across multiple teams' differing constraints |
| Evidence of success | The service's own metrics improved | Other teams independently chose to adopt the same approach without being told to |
| Time horizon | Solved for the current project | Anticipated the next 2–3 projects' needs, not just the one in front of them |

Both are legitimate, strong answers at their respective bars — the risk is a senior-IC-shaped answer given in a staff loop, which reads as under-scoped even when the individual judgment shown was excellent.

Mentorship is frequently under-told in interviews because candidates treat it as soft or unquantifiable, when a strong mentorship story is exactly as evidence-based as a technical one.

Weak: "I mentor junior engineers on my team and try to help them grow." No specifics, no evidence, indistinguishable from someone who's never actually done this.

Strong: "I worked with an engineer for about eight months, starting from mostly executing well-scoped tickets. I deliberately handed them progressively more ambiguous problems — first a small ambiguous bug, then a small feature with an underspecified brief — and reviewed their approach to the ambiguity itself, not just their code. They led their own cross-team initiative within the year and were promoted to senior. I still check in with them roughly monthly, though they no longer need it for day-to-day work."

The strong version treats mentorship like any other body of work: a deliberate approach, a measurable before/after, and a result that outlived the active mentoring period.

slides.sectionTitle: Worked example: the multiplier in numbers
slides.markdown:
A tooling-multiplier story with the numbers made explicit: "I built a contract-testing framework after noticing that roughly a third of our cross-service incidents traced back to undetected API mismatches between a service and its consumers, based on six months of incident tags.

Building it took about three weeks of my time. In the year since, twelve teams have adopted it into their CI pipelines. Cross-service incidents of that specific class dropped from roughly one every three weeks to two in the entire year — and critically, I only directly helped the first two teams adopt it; the other ten found it through internal docs and adopted it without me being involved at all."

The numbers do real work here: three weeks invested, twelve teams' ongoing benefit, a specific incident class's rate before and after, and — the multiplier tell — adoption that happened without the author's continued involvement. A story missing any one of these (the investment, the spread, or the measured effect) is weaker than one that states all three.

slides.sectionTitle: The staff-shaped story that's actually solo work
slides.markdown:
The most common way candidates misfire at this bar: describing a large, individually impressive, individually-executed project as a staff-level story, when the multiplier and through-others elements are simply absent.

A tell: the story is told entirely in terms of what the candidate personally built, with no other engineer's growth, adoption of a pattern, or organizational change mentioned anywhere. "I single-handedly rebuilt our recommendation engine, and it's now 3x faster" is a genuinely strong senior-IC story — it's a weaker staff story unless the candidate can also speak to what happened around it: did anyone else's work change, did the approach get reused, did it require navigating organizational ambiguity beyond the technical problem itself.

The fix isn't to invent multiplier elements that don't exist — it's to be honest about which of your stories are staff-shaped and which are excellent senior-IC stories, and to know the difference before you're asked to distinguish them live.

slides.sectionTitle: Vision without authority to enforce it
slides.markdown:
A staff engineer usually cannot mandate that other teams adopt their technical vision — most staff roles carry influence, not command authority over other teams' roadmaps. This means technical vision has to win by being genuinely the easiest path, not by decree, which is a materially harder bar than simply being right.

A vision that requires every adopting team to do significant extra work up front, with the payoff arriving only much later, will struggle regardless of its technical merit — teams under their own deadline pressure will route around it. A vision that's designed so the easiest, least-effort path for a team building something new is also the one aligned with the broader direction tends to get organic adoption, because it doesn't ask anyone to sacrifice their own short-term goals for the vision's sake.

When telling a technical-vision story, naming how you made adoption the path of least resistance — not just that the vision was correct — is usually the missing piece that makes it land as a staff-level story rather than an unrealized good idea.

Before your next staff-loop interview, audit your story bank against one question per story: **if I removed myself from this story, would anyone else's work, growth, or decisions look different?**

If the honest answer is no — the outcome is entirely a function of your own hours and skill — the story is a strong senior-IC story, and it's worth having a few of those too, since staff+ loops still value technical depth. But your bank needs at least two or three stories where the answer is clearly yes: a mentee who's since grown, a pattern that spread past your involvement, a piece of organizational ambiguity you resolved that nobody else could point to as "assigned" to them.

This single audit question is the fastest way to tell whether your current bank is staff-shaped or a very strong senior portfolio wearing staff-sized language — and it's far better to find that gap before the interview than to discover it under a pointed follow-up question live.
